PsyTrace: A Low-Cost, Easily Deployable Local Platform for College Mental Health Screening Using Questionnaires and Mouse-Trajectory Sensing

PsyTrace combines an eight-scale self-report battery with unobtrusive behavioral sensing — mouse-dynamics features, camera capture, and heart-rate-variability interfaces — on a local-first Tauri 2 / Next.js 14 architecture, delivering bilingual, privacy-preserving screening for college counseling centers — with zero additional hardware, since it relies only on the mouse and webcam already present on screening workstations. It is presented as an engineering contribution with demonstration-level verification; clinical validation is explicitly deferred to future longitudinal work.

Author: Xiang Guo Affiliation: Henan University, Kaifeng, China Contact: guoxiang@henu.edu.cn Manuscript: System paper (draft for submission) Software version: v2.1.0 Code: github.com/GuoXiang9399/PsyPlat (fully open source) Date: 2026-09-18

Abstract

Background. College mental health screening relies almost exclusively on self-report questionnaires, which are vulnerable to recall bias, impression management, and administrative burden. Digital phenotyping — the measurement of behavior through human–computer interaction — offers complementary, passively collected signals, yet few systems integrate it with validated screening scales in a privacy-conscious way. Because the required sensors — the computer mouse and the webcam — are already standard on screening workstations, objective behavioral measurement can be added without any new peripherals such as EEG headsets or wristbands, at near-zero hardware cost.

Objective. We present PsyTrace, a privacy-aware, local-first platform that integrates a multi-scale self-report battery with unobtrusive behavioral sensing to support counseling-center screening workflows.

Methods. PsyTrace is implemented as a Tauri 2 (Rust + WebView) desktop application with a Next.js 14 / TypeScript user interface. Assessment methodology comprises eight built-in validated scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7, C-SSRS, NSSI, PSS-10, PSQI, SIAS-6, ASLEC) plus locally uploaded custom scales, a four-tier risk taxonomy with per-scale adjustable thresholds, and crisis-first escalation of positive suicidal-risk indicators. Behavioral sensing captures mouse trajectories throughout the questionnaire (14 kinematic features, 5 heuristic signals), a camera feed at 320×240 with automatic degraded-mode fallback, and an HRV interface contract. All records, videos, and settings persist locally (SQLite, IndexedDB), and exports support privacy-masking modes.

Results. The full screening workflow — informed consent, silent sensing, four-tier risk classification, per-scale risk dashboards, exploratory correlation analytics, and privacy-aware report export — is demonstrated end-to-end. Engineering verification includes successful type-checking, a production build, and 26 DOM-level smoke tests; the interface ships with 545+ translation keys in Chinese and English. The platform is fully open source, and the complete source code is available on GitHub.

Conclusions. PsyTrace demonstrates a feasible engineering foundation for multimodal, privacy-preserving college mental health screening. Running on ubiquitous hardware with no additional peripherals, it is also a low-cost, easily promotable screening infrastructure. It is a research prototype, not a diagnostic device: calibration of heuristic thresholds and clinical validation with longitudinal cohorts are required next steps.

Keywords

digital phenotyping mouse dynamics mental health screening college students behavioral sensing privacy-preserving platform

1. Introduction

Mental disorders are among the most prevalent health problems in higher education. Cross-national estimates from the WHO World Mental Health Surveys International College Student Project indicate that roughly one in three first-year college students screens positive for at least one common mental disorder, with mood, anxiety, and substance-use conditions dominating the distribution[8]. The WHO further reports that half of all mental health conditions begin by age 14 and three-quarters by the mid-20s, placing the university years in the highest-risk window[9]. Counseling centers therefore conduct routine screening at scale, and the timeliness of detection — before crises such as suicidal ideation escalate — is a first-order operational concern.

Standard screening instruments, including the PHQ-9[1] and GAD-7[2], are brief, validated, and widely adopted, yet they inherit the intrinsic limits of self-report: recall error over the reference window, social-desirability bias, and reduced validity in low-effort responding. In parallel, the concept of digital phenotyping — the moment-by-moment quantification of individual behavior from the data produced by human–computer interaction — has matured as a complement to clinical scales[7][15]. Passive behavioral streams (keystroke and mouse dynamics, speech, mobility) have been shown to carry information about mood, psychomotor state, and engagement, motivating their incorporation into screening platforms. Importantly, the sensors needed for such measurement — the pointing device and the webcam — are already ubiquitous on screening workstations: unlike EEG headsets or smart wristbands, no dedicated wearable or new peripheral is required, so the marginal hardware cost of adding objective measurement is effectively zero. Because these streams are produced by the respondent's actual interaction rather than by retrospective recall, they constitute an objective complement to questionnaire scores, mitigating the self-report biases noted above.

However, most existing platforms are server-centric: questionnaire data, behavioral streams, and video recordings transit a remote backend, raising privacy concerns that are especially acute for mental-health data and for sensitive sub-populations such as suicidal ideation screening. Furthermore, few systems couple a complete screening workflow — consent, unobtrusive sensing, multi-scale risk classification, case management, and report export — inside one coherent application.

We designed PsyTrace to close this gap. The platform (i) keeps all personal data local on the device by default; (ii) layers mouse-dynamics and camera sensing onto an existing validated scale battery without changing the respondent's interaction model; (iii) exposes a transparent, threshold-configurable four-tier risk model with crisis-first escalation of positive suicidal-risk indicators; and (iv) provides bilingual (Chinese/English) interfaces for global deployment. The main contributions of this work are:

  • 1A local-first architecture combining Tauri 2 (Rust) and Next.js 14, where assessment records, behavioral streams, settings, and camera videos persist exclusively on-device (SQLite + IndexedDB), with optional privacy-masked exports.
  • 2A multi-scale screening methodology with eight built-in validated instruments, custom-scale upload (JSON/TXT), a four-tier risk taxonomy, per-scale adjustable thresholds, and crisis-first escalation that prioritizes positive suicidal-risk indicators above the general severity pipeline.
  • 3A behavior-sensing pipeline that computes 14 mouse-dynamics features and 5 rule-based behavioral signals during the questionnaire, together with a camera capture module (320×240) with degraded-mode fallback and an HRV interface contract.
  • 4An exploratory analysis workbench for counseling staff — per-scale risk distributions, behavior-signal × risk cross-tabulations, and scale–behavior correlation heatmaps — plus privacy-aware CSV/JSON/HTML report export.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 describes the system design and architecture. Section 4 presents the assessment methodology, and Section 5 the behavioral sensing and feature engineering. Section 6 covers data management, analysis, and export. Section 7 reports engineering evaluation and demonstration, Section 8 discusses implications, and Section 9 states limitations and future work. Section 10 concludes.

2. Related Work

2.1 Digital phenotyping and behavior-based screening

Insel articulated digital phenotyping as a means to capture behavior unobtrusively from personal digital devices, arguing that such data could complement clinician- and self-report-based assessment[7]. Onnela and Rauch extended the agenda to smartphones, demonstrating passive collection of sociality, mobility, and phone use as correlates of mental state[15]. Platform-level contributions include the Beiwe research platform, which provides configurable active and passive sensing for psychiatric studies[14]. PsyTrace differs in its deployment target: rather than smartphone-based longitudinal observation, it focuses on synchronous screening sessions in a counseling-center workflow, where the sensing window is the questionnaire itself, and — unlike wristband- or EEG-based approaches — it depends only on the input devices already attached to the workstation.

2.2 Mouse dynamics as a behavioral signal

Mouse dynamics — the kinematics of pointing-device movement — was introduced as a behavioral biometric, using features such as movement speed, acceleration, and direction reversals to verify identity[12]. Subsequent work linked these kinematics to psychological constructs: psychomotor slowing is a hallmark of depression[10], and motor variability has been associated with attentional state. PsyTrace operationalizes these findings as a compact feature set (speed, pauses, direction reversals, curvature, tremor-like micro-movements) and combines them into interpretable rule-based signals rather than opaque classifiers, preserving explainability for non-technical counseling staff.

2.3 Physiological signals: HRV and sleep

Heart-rate variability (HRV) reflects prefrontal inhibitory control over brainstem circuits and has been proposed as an index of self-regulation and emotional state[11]. Sleep quality, measurable via the PSQI[4], is both a transdiagnostic risk factor and a modifiable treatment target[13]. PsyTrace includes the PSQI in its battery and exposes an HRV interface contract in its sensing layer for wearable or webcam-based photoplethysmography sources.

2.4 Web-based screening platforms and privacy

Web-based screening has demonstrated reach and efficiency, but server-mediated storage of mental-health data raises disclosure risks. PsyTrace's design choice — local-first storage with explicit, privacy-masked export — addresses this concern at the architectural level rather than through policy alone.

3. System Design and Architecture

3.1 Design goals

Six goals drove the design: G1 privacy by default (no server round-trip for personal data); G2 zero-training usability for both respondents and counseling staff; G3 sensing that is unobtrusive — respondents answer questionnaires exactly as usual; G4 extensible assessment content (enable/disable scales, adjust thresholds, upload custom scales); G5 international usability via full bilingual (zh/en) localization; and G6 zero marginal hardware — sensing relies solely on the mouse and webcam already present on screening workstations, so objective measurement adds no equipment cost.

3.2 Architecture

PsyTrace is a desktop application built with Tauri 2, whose Rust core hosts the system services and a WebView rendering the Next.js 14 / TypeScript front end. The front end is organized into seven route modules — Overview, Assessment, Assessment Setup, Data Management, Analysis, Settings, and About — sharing a common shell and language-aware sidebar. The Rust layer exposes an IPC bridge (Tokio async runtime), an embedded SQLite store for assessment records and settings, and interface contracts for OpenCV-based facial detection and HRV analysis. Camera video captured during assessment is persisted to IndexedDB in the WebView as WebM files. Figure 1 shows the layered architecture.

3.3 Local-first data model

Every assessment record bundles questionnaire answers, per-scale scores, risk labels, mouse trajectory, derived behavior metrics and signals, camera mode, and video references. Records are written transactionally on completion and remain queryable for the analysis workbench. The same local store holds assessment settings (enabled scales, thresholds, custom scales), guaranteeing that configuration and data stay co-located on the device.

4. Assessment Methodology

4.1 Scale battery

PsyTrace ships with eight built-in scales covering the principal domains of a college screening intake: depression (PHQ-9[1]), generalized anxiety (GAD-7[2]), suicidal risk (C-SSRS[3]), non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), perceived stress (PSS-10[5]), sleep quality (PSQI[4]), social interaction anxiety (SIAS-6[6]), and negative life events (ASLEC). Administrators may enable or disable each scale independently and upload additional custom scales from JSON or TXT files. Table 1 summarizes the battery and its default severity cutoffs.

Table 1. Built-in scale battery, reference windows, and default four-tier cutoffs.

Scale Items Reference window Primary construct Default cutoffs (low / mild / moderate / high)
PHQ-99Past 2 weeksDepression severity0–4 / 5–9 / 10–14 / ≥15
GAD-77Past 2 weeksGeneralized anxiety0–4 / 5–9 / 10–14 / ≥15
C-SSRS (screen)4Past monthSuicidal ideation / behaviorAny positive item → high
NSSI2Past yearNon-suicidal self-injuryNone → low; yes → moderate; + PHQ-9 item 9 → high
PSS-1010Past monthPerceived stress0–13 / 14–19 / 20–26 / ≥27
PSQI19 (7 components)Past monthSleep quality0–5 / 6–10 / 11–15 / ≥16
SIAS-66Past 2 weeksSocial interaction anxiety0–6 / 7–12 / 13–18 / ≥19
ASLEC27Past yearNegative life events (impact)0–15 / 16–35 / 36–60 / ≥61
Custom scalesUser-defined—Administrator-definedAdjustable per scale

Cutoffs are configurable per scale in Assessment Setup under the constraint mild ≤ moderate ≤ severe; values shown are the shipped defaults, aligned with common scoring practice. C-SSRS and NSSI are binary screening scales (positive-indicator alerts) and are not user-adjustable.

4.2 Four-tier risk model with crisis-first escalation

Each scale is scored independently into a four-tier risk label — low, mild, moderate, high — against its thresholds. The overall risk is the maximum level of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores. Crisis-relevant indicators override the general severity pipeline: any positive C-SSRS item is treated as high risk with a suicide flag, and NSSI positivity as moderate, escalated to high when the concurrent PHQ-9 item 9 (self-harm ideation) is endorsed. The stress, sleep, social-anxiety, and life-event scales contribute context to the record without overriding this core signal. Figure 2 formalizes this logic.

4.3 Consent and sensing authorization

The workflow begins with basic demographic capture and an informed-consent step that explains data use, sensing, storage, and the right to abort at any time. Camera access is requested once at the consent step (pre-authorization); if the respondent declines, or if no camera is present or the request times out (8 s), the system switches to a degraded mode in which assessment continues without video — the response flow is never blocked by sensing failure. Figure 3 shows the four-step assessment workflow.

5. Behavioral Sensing and Feature Engineering

5.1 Mouse-trajectory collection

The sensing modalities were chosen for pervasiveness: the computer mouse and the webcam are present on virtually every screening workstation, whereas EEG headsets and smart wristbands would add procurement, maintenance, and compliance burden. PsyTrace therefore captures objective behavioral data with zero additional hardware. During questionnaire answering, the platform samples pointer position (x, y) with timestamps on every movement and records click events. The raw stream is compressed into a trajectory of points and consumed by the feature extractor; the same stream is visualized in Data Management for staff inspection. Table 2 lists the 14 derived kinematic features.

Table 2. Mouse-dynamics feature set computed from the trajectory.

Feature Definition Unit
durationTotal elapsed time from first to last samplems
pointsNumber of sampled trajectory pointscount
clicksNumber of click events recordedcount
distanceCumulative Euclidean displacement between consecutive samplespx
avgSpeedMean inter-sample speedpx/ms
speedCVCoefficient of variation of inter-sample speedratio
maxSpeedPeak inter-sample speedpx/ms
pauseCountHover-like pauses: displacement < 24 px with interval > 600 mscount
pauseRatioShare of pause duration in total durationratio
initLatencyLatency from session start to first movement > 24 pxms
xFlips / yFlipsHorizontal / vertical direction reversals of significant movementscount
curvaturePath length divided by straight-line distance (≥ 1)ratio
tremorScoreCount of high-frequency micro-directional reversals (interval < 120 ms, small amplitude)score

Features are computed by a pure function over the trajectory (minimum three points); thresholds embedded in the definitions are heuristic and calibratable as data accumulate.

5.2 Behavioral signal heuristics

Rather than a black-box classifier, PsyTrace maps features to five interpretable signals using explicit rules grounded in the clinical literature — psychomotor slowing in depression[10], indecision, attentional fluctuation, and fine-motor instability. Each signal carries a plain-language label and an explicit advisory (e.g., "suggest review"), making the output usable by non-technical staff while remaining transparently inspectable. Table 3 lists the rules.

Table 3. Rule-based behavioral signals and their decision rules.

Signal Decision rule (heuristic) Rationale
low_effortduration < max(60 s, 0.5 × baseline) ∧ clicks < 5 ∧ pauseRatio < 0.05Rapid, click-sparse completion flags response-validity review
retardationavgSpeed < 0.12 ∧ pauseRatio > 0.35 ∧ initLatency > 1500 msSlow movement with long initial latency matches psychomotor slowing[10]
hesitationcurvature > 1.9 ∧ (xFlips + yFlips) > 8 ∧ pauseCount > 6Tortuous paths with reversals and pauses indicate indecision
mind_wanderingspeedCV > 1.8 ∧ curvature > 1.6High speed variability with drifting paths suggests attentional fluctuation
tremortremorScore > 10 ∧ moving samples > 40Frequent micro-reversals indicate fine-motor instability (weak signal)

All signals are heuristic advisories for staff triage; they do not constitute diagnosis and must be interpreted together with scale scores.

5.3 Camera capture and degraded mode

With consent, the camera records the answer session at 320×240 into WebM files in IndexedDB. If permission is denied, no camera exists, or the 8 s authorization times out, the session runs in degraded mode: assessment continues normally and the record stores cameraMode = degraded with no video. An in-app calibration panel lets administrators verify permission, stream, and fallback behavior against a real capture, mirroring the exact session logic.

5.4 HRV interface contract

An HRV analysis contract is defined in the Rust core to accept R-R interval series (e.g., from webcam-based photoplethysmography or wearables) and return time-domain metrics such as sample entropy. The interface is currently stubbed for demonstration and is wired for future multimodal fusion.

6. Data Management, Analysis, and Export

6.1 Record dashboard and per-scale risk

Data Management presents every record with all per-scale scores and independent risk labels in a sortable table, plus search and multi-dimension filtering (overall risk and each scale's risk). A detail view reconstructs the full answer sheet, the early-warning summary, behavior metrics, and the raw mouse trajectory rendered as an SVG path with start/end markers.

6.2 Exploratory analysis workbench

The Analysis module supports targetable analysis over selected records: sample composition by risk and camera mode; per-scale risk distributions; trajectory-feature distributions; behavior-signal × risk-level cross-tabulation; scale–trajectory correlation heatmaps; and camera-status × scale-score comparisons. These visualizations are explicitly heuristic ("exploratory analysis for staff reference, not clinical diagnosis") and render without external charting dependencies.

6.3 Export with privacy modes

Exports support CSV, JSON, and self-contained HTML reports, each with a privacy-masking toggle that de-identifies student IDs and personal fields. Video can be exported as independent WebM files with an explicit handling warning, since recordings contain facial imagery. Per-record HTML reports are generated for individual case review, with the same privacy toggle.

Interpretation caveat Risk labels, behavioral signals, and correlation analyses produced by PsyTrace are heuristic and advisory. They are intended to prioritize staff review, not to render clinical judgments; any service decision requires professional evaluation of the full record.

7. Engineering Evaluation and Demonstration

7.1 Verification suite

The front end passes strict TypeScript checking (tsc --noEmit) and a production next build. A DOM-level smoke-test harness exercises the critical paths — section switching, selection-count changes, report export for single- and multi-record cases, PDF print flow, per-record report modals, and language switching — all 26 assertions passing with no undefined or NaN artifacts. The i18n layer maintains 545+ keys across Chinese and English, and the document title and meta description update with the active language.

7.2 Demonstration dataset

A demonstration dataset of eight anonymized records covers the full risk spectrum, including C-SSRS-positive (suicide-flag) and NSSI-positive cases with concurrent PHQ-9 item-9 endorsement, plus realistic mouse trajectories with embedded behavioral signals. This dataset drives every module of the platform and doubles as acceptance fixtures for the smoke tests.

7.3 End-to-end workflow demonstration

The demonstrated flow is: administrator enables scales and adjusts thresholds → respondent completes basic info, consents, and answers the battery (with silent mouse sampling and camera capture) → the record is archived with per-scale risks and signals → staff filter, inspect, and export privacy-masked reports or a PDF. The complete flow runs locally with zero network dependencies.

We deliberately do not report clinical accuracy metrics: the system has not yet been validated against clinician-administered gold standards, and any such figures would be premature and misleading.

8. Discussion

PsyTrace occupies a specific niche among digital phenotyping platforms: synchronous, in-office screening rather than longitudinal smartphone observation. Compared with server-centric screening suites, its local-first storage directly addresses the disclosure risk that is amplified when mental-health data — particularly suicide-risk indicators — are transmitted and stored remotely. The architecture also reduces deployment cost: no backend provisioning is required for a counseling center, and data retention is governed by local policy.

The early-warning logic encodes a defensible clinical-prioritization principle: crisis indicators (C-SSRS, NSSI) outrank general severity scores, and the remaining scales (PSS-10, PSQI, SIAS-6, ASLEC) provide context rather than overriding the core signal. Keeping per-scale risk independent of the overall label supports the multi-dimensional review that counselors actually perform — a depressed respondent with good sleep and a sleeping-problem respondent without mood symptoms are distinguishable at a glance.

The choice of rule-based behavioral signals over machine-learned classifiers reflects a deliberate trade-off. Rules are transparent, auditable, and can be calibrated by a center's own data; they will, however, underperform tuned models when large labeled corpora become available. The feature set (Table 2) is intentionally compact and theory-grounded, easing that future transition.

The deployment economics of the platform are unusually favorable for a digital-phenotyping system. Because it requires no dedicated hardware — the mouse and webcam are already present — and no server infrastructure, the incremental cost of a screening station is effectively the cost of the software itself; this combination of zero marginal hardware cost and local-first operation makes the system straightforward to promote across resource-constrained university counseling centers. The sensor streams also play an important epistemic role: they are generated by the respondent's real-time interaction rather than by retrospective recall, so they offer an objective complement to questionnaire scores, flagging low-effort responding, psychomotor slowing, or hesitation that self-report alone would conceal.

9. Limitations and Future Work

The most important limitation is the absence of clinical validation. Thresholds and signal rules are heuristic defaults; their sensitivity and specificity against structured clinical interviews are unknown. Second, behavioral signals are session-level and may reflect device, desk ergonomics, or transient state rather than stable traits — a confound that only longitudinal within-subject designs can resolve. Third, camera-based recording, even consent-based and local-only, carries residual privacy and social-acceptability risk; the degraded-mode path mitigates but does not eliminate it. Fourth, the current evaluation is an engineering demonstration with synthetic acceptance data, not a field trial.

Future work proceeds along three tracks: (1) a longitudinal cohort study comparing PsyTrace risk labels and behavioral signals against clinician-administered gold standards to calibrate thresholds and report real accuracy; (2) an incremental machine-learning fusion layer over the existing feature set, with explainability constraints; and (3) deployment engineering — remote consent management, encrypted backup, and institutional integration. An open question is whether synchronous sensing at screening time carries incremental validity beyond the scales themselves; the correlation workbench in PsyTrace is designed to make exactly this question answerable with collected data.

10. Conclusion

We presented PsyTrace, a privacy-aware, local-first platform that integrates an eight-scale screening battery with unobtrusive behavioral sensing for college mental health. Its contributions lie in a deployable architecture that keeps sensitive data on-device, a transparent four-tier risk model with crisis-first escalation, a compact and interpretable mouse-dynamics feature and signal set, and an exploratory analysis workbench for counseling staff. The system is a validated engineering prototype with a complete demonstration; the decisive next step is clinical validation with longitudinal cohorts, for which the platform's data and export infrastructure are already prepared. The platform is fully open source and publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/GuoXiang9399/PsyPlat).

Code Availability

PsyTrace is fully open source. The complete source code — the Tauri 2 Rust core, the Next.js 14 front end, the built-in scale battery with its scoring logic, the demonstration dataset, and the smoke-test harness — is available on GitHub at https://github.com/GuoXiang9399/PsyPlat, enabling other institutions to inspect, audit, and reuse the platform.
